For me at least, 'It'll be the Sites for us on the 26th' doesn't translate into 'it'll be back to work for us on the 26th'. Why 'the Sites', plural? Hu Zhi's tale is about Site-19; according to your member pages, Hu Zhi works in Hong-Kong, and Hu An in Sarawak. Do you mean they're planning to tour some sites after the holidays?

Ah, I mean 'Sites' as a general term for 'working in the Foundation' (since the Sites are the default Foundation workplace). The characters here have nothing to do with Site-19, although 19's significance in the Foundation makes it a more archetypal story.

But hell yeah, them being transferred to other sites after Christmas is not an impossibility.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
No, no, MrWrong, you've got it wrong.
055 is not a sphere.
And Santa is not a sphere either.
Ergo, Santa is 055.

We could use some cold here too. Some plants in the garden are blooming. And if it goes on like this, we shall be completely invaded by instances of SCP-006-J (especially SCP-006-J-1, the stupid little fuckers) by March.

Now. May I nitpick about a few things, my tropical friend? ;>

+ show block
– hide block

I've noticed recently a few tales that mix up sentences in present tense and in past tense. It never fails to disturb me. IMO, you can do this, but it has to be deliberate and meaningful, for effect: for instance, to suddenly speed up a scene when some action takes place.
So, I would put all these sentences in past tense:

He was a fairly obese man of pale complexion, with round chest and belly. Donned in red and white, he was silent and stealthy. In his hands, he carried an equally round red sack that rattled and jingled every step the man took. This man was Santa, obviously.

OTOH, I wouldn't object to this being in present tense:

But suddenly…
"Hey there!" a voice cries.
Santa turns around calmly and he sees a young boy, most likely aged between six to nine. The young boy is holding an action figure of a brass robot, worn with age – the many years it has been in this boy's possession. The young boy stares blankly at this stout stranger in front of him, trying his hardest not to blink.

then back to past tense…!

Also, I think sometimes you tend to spell everything out, which weighs down your style and story. For instance:

But in the end, the temptation to blink was too potent and the boy blinked. Santa was no longer by the Christmas tree; he was right in front of the boy with gift box still in hand. He bent down again and presented the boy with the gift box.

This way, the storytelling is quicker and lighter, with no repetition. What do you think?

"Little Fred, I presume? Take it."
The boy – named Fred – accepted the gift box, dropping his brass action figure in the process. He shook the box, thinking wondering what it could be. All this time, Santa looked on with a gentle smile on his face.

The mother is going to call him Fred a few lines further down: you could easily do without this "- named Fred".

You could switch again to present tense for the mother's appearance, for fun effect.

The hallways of Site-19 are long and winding, although Santa knew his way around well enough.

For some reason, present tense looks right here, even if you switch back to past in the same sentence. Don't ask me why. Please. Just feels right!!!!
Same with this:

The door opened on its own accord, as though it noticed Santa's presence. Inside is an empty room of concrete with a Faraday cage. Santa entered the room

Yeah. The mysteries of good writing…!

He entered the cells of one his assigned SCPs, in a room with a Faraday cage Inside

Should be:
He entered the cell of one of his assigned SCPs: a room with a Faraday cage inside
What do you think?

a bit of humour and entertainment keep us sane

Should be 'keeps us sane' (subject of the verb is 'bit', = singular)

Besides, it'll be the Sites for us on the 26th

What do you mean?

Even father couldn't convince him to

Should be Father

The door bell to the Hu residence rang, while An kept on typing.

This (and the rest of the paragraph) could be in present tense again.

I must say I don't quite understand the link between the two parts of your tale (Santa -> the Hu family), but… hey, why not?

No vote for now. I do believe your tale needs a wee bit of tightening up!

Oh, BTW: I'm rather surprised that Santa Claus is not already an SCP with its own huge canon hub… Or have I not searched properly? ;>

item.title: Merry Christmas Coldpost
item.content:encoded:
I usually don't do this, but since it's the Christmas season and me living in the not-cold tropics, I need some coldness in my life. Hence the coldpost as my little something for Christmas!

SCPs mentioned here include: SCP-055 by qntm

The Hu siblings are taken from my author page.

– hide block

SCP-055 is not round. Since it is an anti-meme that hides its own traits, what if the one trait we all know it to not be is actually 055's most definitive trait (being round).

Ergo, SCP-055 is actually round.

For elaboration,

055 has been called a weak anti-meme, since we can still know that it is at least known. If it really was a weak anti-meme, 055 would be doing a shitty job at obscuring itself. While that is usually represented by "We can deduce what it is not" logic, this rides on the "a weak anti-meme that somehow has everyone remember just one trait that it actually has yet has it framed it as what it should not be".

e.g. Santa!055 is actually round –> Person sees Santa!055 –> Person forgets everything about Santa!055 due to antimemetic aspects, except the roundness (due to weak anti-meme) –> Antimemetic aspects still manage to force Person to dismiss roundness as a trait Santa!055 does not have –> Person says, "Santa!055 is not round".
